newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: White S.African leader negotiates amnesty plea.
newsitem.headline: White S.African leader negotiates amnesty plea.

text.p: A white right-wing leader who preached restraint to khaki-clad extremists during South Africa's first all-race election in 1994 announced on Monday he was negotiating a possible amnesty plea.

Constand Viljoen, leader of the Freedom Party, told state radio he had held preliminary discussions with the "truth commission" on an abortive pre-election plot by the white right which envisaged the use of violence to gain their own homeland.

He gave no details on any actions which might have been carried out under the campaign, but said he did not intend to seek amnesty for violent acts committed by his followers, nor for any actions committed while he was chief of the army.

Nine right-wingers were convicted last year for planting bombs in and around Johannesburg that killed 20 people shortly before the April 1994 election. The men were members of the neo-Nazi Afrikaner Resistance Movement.

Viljoen headed the apartheid defence force in the 1970s and 1980s after black township uprisings, executing a military crusade against black liberation movements at home and cross-border raids in neighbouring black states.

Shortly before the historic election which ushered President Nelson Mandela into power, Viljoen began to unite a splintered white right-wing behind non-violence, gaining respect from many political observers as a pragmatic and rational leader.
Nobel peace laureate Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, probing apartheid abuses, has the authority to grant amnesty to perpetrators if they make a full confession.
